measurement.happened:
This week in Iraq was dominated by three interlocking stories that together paint a picture of a country being squeezed between a collapsing internal power arrangement in the north and a widening US-Iran confrontation that Baghdad is trying to navigate without picking a side.

First, the Kurdish power-sharing deal fell apart. On November 5, the Associated Press reported that one of the two rival Kurdish parties quit the northern government, cracking the coalition that had held Erbil and Sulaymaniyah together. By November 8, Al Jazeera was asking openly whether the Kurdish region could return to two separate administrations, the way it was before the 2020s-era unity government. This is not a small footnote. For years the PUK and KDP have shared power in a fragile arrangement, and one party walking out means the cabinet is now either a minority or effectively dead, with budget disputes, ministerial vacancies, and a public narrative of 'two governments in Kurdistan' gaining traction. The TV5Monde piece on French jihadists expressing 'regrets' while being judged in Baghdad for their Syrian past is a small side-note, but it reminds us that the federal justice system is still working through the post-ISIS backlog, a quiet thread running alongside the louder political drama.

Second, drones hit Kurdish energy and opposition targets. On November 4, Reuters reported drone strikes on Iranian Kurdish opposition groups in Sulaymaniyah and east Erbil. Then on November 8, the Khor Mor gas field was hit by a drone attack and production was halted, confirmed by the operator and picked up by both Reuters and Al Jazeera. By November 9, Al Jazeera reported that the loss of Khor Mor gas triggered a mass blackout across parts of Iraqi Kurdistan. This is significant because Khor Mor is one of the largest gas supplies feeding the Kurdish power grid; losing it in late autumn, when heating demand is rising, turns a military strike into an immediate quality-of-life crisis for hundreds of thousands of people. The pattern of attacks, first on opposition groups, then on infrastructure, suggests a deliberate escalation by an actor (most likely Iran or a proxy) that wants to punish the Kurdish region for hosting opposition figures and to weaken its economic base.

Third, the US-Iran-Iraq triangle tightened. On November 8, Reuters reported that the US asked Iraq to shut most of its border crossings with Iran, something the Iraqi foreign minister confirmed. The same day, an Iraqi minister said Baghdad had reached understandings with Washington to keep oil exports flowing through the Strait of Hormuz. Al Jazeera on November 6 explained that Iran was exempting India, China, Qatar, and Iraq from its Hormuz restrictions, which means Iraq is getting a rare pass in a broader energy chokepoint crisis. On November 6, Al Jazeera also reported that Iraq's foreign minister al-Zaidi was in talks with President Trump as Baghdad sought to stay out of a potential US-Iran war. On November 7, al-Zaidi publicly said 'external parties' were using Iraqi soil to attack neighbours, a diplomatic way of pointing fingers at both Iran (for launching drones) and possibly the US (for staging operations or intelligence on Iraqi territory) without naming names.

Taken together, the week shows Iraq in a classic sandwich: the north is politically fracturing and physically being bombed, the centre is trying to keep the federal government functional, and the whole country is being pulled into a US-Iran standoff that Baghdad does not want to join but cannot fully avoid.
measurement.expected:
Looking at the next seven days, November 9 through roughly November 16, here is what I expect, theme by theme.

Kurdish politics: It is almost certain that the political crisis in Iraqi Kurdistan will dominate headlines. With one party out of the government, the remaining coalition will either try to govern on a minority basis, trigger a vote of no confidence, or call a snap election. Expect a flurry of cabinet reshuffles, public statements from both the PUK and KDP leadership, and back-channel talks to see if a new deal can be stitched together before the blackouts and gas shortages make the public angry enough to demand action. It is probable that at least one more minister resigns or is dismissed in the coming days. It is possible, though not certain, that both parties announce a framework for a new power-sharing agreement within the week, but given the tone of the Al Jazeera 'two administrations' headline, a full re-merger is less likely than a managed split or a very narrow coalition.

Energy and blackouts: It is almost certain that the Khor Mor gas field remains offline or in only partial operation through at least the end of the week, since gas-field repairs after a drone strike typically take days to assess and weeks to fully restore. It is probable that Kurdish regions experience repeated or prolonged blackouts, especially in the evenings, and that the federal government in Baghdad steps in to coordinate emergency fuel or gas deliveries from the south. It is possible that a second drone strike hits another energy or opposition target before the week is out, particularly if Iran wants to signal that the first hit was a warning. It is unlikely that full production resumes before November 16.

US-Iran-Iraq diplomacy: It is probable that Iraq begins a visible, if partial, closure of its main border crossings with Iran, as the US has requested. This will be politically painful for Iraq because those crossings are a major trade and smuggling artery, and border towns will feel the impact quickly. Expect the Iraqi foreign ministry to issue statements about 'phased' or 'targeted' closures rather than a full shutdown. It is almost certain that al-Zaidi or another senior Iraqi official makes at least one more high-profile contact with Washington, Tehran, or both, to keep Baghdad in the middle and avoid being drafted into a formal side. It is possible that Iraq announces the specific terms of its Hormuz oil-export arrangement with the US, including volumes, timelines, and any fee or transit-fee structure. It is unlikely that a formal US-Iran-Iraq trilateral meeting happens within seven days, but bilateral phone calls are near-certain to continue.

Federal politics in Baghdad: It is probable that the federal cabinet holds an emergency or special session to address the Kurdish crisis, the border closures, and the energy disruption. It is possible that the prime minister makes a public address to reassure Iraqis that Baghdad is in control and not being dragged into a US-Iran war. It is unlikely that a major no-confidence vote or cabinet collapse happens in Baghdad itself within this window, but the pressure is building.

Security and public mood: It is probable that the mass blackouts in the Kurdish regions generate street protests or at least loud social-media outrage, especially if they persist into the second week. It is possible that a small protest or sit-in appears in Erbil or Sulaymaniyah calling for the government to act. It is less likely that violence spreads to Baghdad or the south within seven days unless a new drone strike or a border-closure dispute triggers it.

Less likely surprises I would keep on my radar: a sudden snap-election announcement in the Kurdish region (possible but would need a legal trigger); a major corruption or bribery scandal involving one of the Kurdish parties that accelerates the split; a flash flood or early cold snap in the north that compounds the blackout misery; a second wave of drone attacks on federal (not just Kurdish) infrastructure, which would shift the blame narrative in Baghdad; and a brief but loud US military operation or airstrike on a target in or near Iraq that the US then calls 'self-defence.'

Things I would not bet on in this seven-day window: a full-scale ground war involving Iraqi federal troops; a constitutional referendum or major legislative overhaul in Baghdad; a change of prime minister in Baghdad; a formal Iraqi entry into a US or Iranian military alliance; a complete Hormuz closure that specifically targets Iraqi tankers (given the exemption already granted); and a peaceful, fully implemented new Kurdish power-sharing deal signed and celebrated before November 16. The political and physical damage is too fresh and the parties too angry for a neat resolution this quickly.
emoji_reasons: The drone strike on the Khor Mor gas field and the resulting mass blackout across Iraqi Kurdistan is the most immediately felt, concrete event of the week, turning a military attack into a daily-life crisis for hundreds of thousands of people.

The collapse of the Kurdish power-sharing deal, with one major party quitting the government and the open question of whether the region will split into two administrations again, is the biggest structural political shift of the week.

The constant diplomatic shuttle, with Iraq's foreign minister talking to Trump, the US asking for border closures, and Baghdad negotiating its Hormuz oil exemption, shows that Iraq is living in a phone-call-and-handshake diplomacy mode, trying to stay out of a war it did not start.

delta.motion: Between the two photographs, the security theme grew dramatically in both scope and severity. In the first photo, the drone threat was a single intercepted craft near Baghdad's Green Zone, a contained near-miss. By the second photo, drones had struck Kurdish opposition groups in Sulaymaniyah and east Erbil, then hit the Khor Mor gas field, halting production and triggering a mass blackout across parts of Iraqi Kurdistan. The threat moved from the centre to the north, from a single interception to repeated strikes on both political and economic targets, and the consequences shifted from a nervous official statement to hundreds of thousands of people losing power in late autumn. The US-Iran-Iraq triangle grew from a quiet Wall Street Journal note about wind-down transactions with an Iran-linked bank into a full diplomatic realignment: Washington formally asked Baghdad to close most of its border crossings with Tehran, Iraq secured a rare Hormuz exemption, and Prime Minister al-Zaidi was in direct talks with President Trump. The banking story became a border-and-chokepoint story. The Kurdish internal politics theme also grew, but in a different direction. In the first photo the north was consolidating: PKK-linked Yazidi units were disarming and joining the army, a sign of Baghdad asserting unified command. By the second photo the coalition in Erbil had cracked, one of the two major Kurdish parties had quit, and Al Jazeera was openly asking whether the region would split into two separate administrations again. The energy theme shifted from opportunity to crisis: the first photo carried the optimistic DNO exploration of a Syria pipeline, while the second photo carried the loss of Khor Mor gas and a resulting blackout. Several themes shrank or vanished entirely. The French life-sentence story, which dominated the first photo with coverage across at least seven outlets, shrank to a single TV5Monde side-note about the defendants expressing regrets. The Tishreen seventh-anniversary pulse, the Pope's Mosul visit, the Christian community's tentative return, the corruption-verdict appeals, the Syria re-engagement (the PM's Damascus meeting, the DNO pipeline talks), and the PKK-linked Yazidi disarmament all disappeared from the second photo's headlines, swallowed by the louder Kurdish fracture and the US-Iran standoff. What appeared fresh in the second photo was the specific combination of a Kurdish coalition collapse, a gas-field strike causing a blackout, a formal US request to close border crossings, a named Hormuz exemption for Iraq, and the PM's diplomatic language about external parties using Iraqi soil. None of these were present in the first photo, and together they mark a shift from a week of court verdicts and diplomatic gestures to a week of structural stress and external pressure.
delta.wind: On the French diplomatic reaction, the expectation was a formal Quai d'Orsay statement, consular access requests, and possibly a parliamentary debate. What actually happened was quieter: the story shrank to a TV5Monde piece in which the French defendants expressed regrets while being judged. France stayed in the news, as predicted, but the diplomatic firestorm did not materialise in this week's headlines. The expectation was partly right in form (the story persisted in French media) but overestimated in intensity. On the Tishreen anniversary follow-through, the expectation was a few more local stories and possibly small demonstrations. The reality was silence: the anniversary simply faded from the news cycle by November 9, exactly as the 'unlikely' scenario suggested. This came true as expected. On the corruption-case fallout, the expectation was appeals, political posturing, and questions about the DNO pipeline. None of that appeared in the second photo. The story was overtaken by the Kurdish coalition collapse and the US-Iran crisis, and the appeals either happened quietly or were still pending. The expectation was reasonable but the story was simply too small to compete. On the Pope and Christian community, the expectation was continued coverage and small services. The absence in the second photo makes sense: it is still November, the 'bittersweet first Christmas' theme is weeks away, and the Mosul visit was a one-time event. The expectation was slightly too generous for this specific seven-day window. On the Kurdistan oil via Syria, the expectation was a technical update or press release confirming ongoing talks. That did not appear. Instead, the energy narrative shifted entirely: the DNO Syria pipeline story was replaced by the Khor Mor gas field strike and the resulting blackout. The expectation was reasonable but the energy story changed character from new opportunity to existing vulnerability. On security around Baghdad, the expectation was a possible second drone and visible nervousness in official statements. The drone threat did grow, but it moved from the Green Zone to Kurdish infrastructure. The nervousness was real, but it was expressed through the PM's 'external parties' remark and the US border-crossing request rather than through a second Baghdad interception. The expectation was directionally correct but geographically misplaced. On the PKK-linked Yazidi disarmament, the expectation was incremental logistical news. The story continued in the background but was overshadowed by the bigger Kurdish political fracture. The expectation was reasonable but the smaller story could not compete with the coalition collapse. On banking and Iran linkages, the expectation was a possible central-bank follow-up. What actually happened was far larger: the US formally asked Iraq to close border crossings, Iraq got a named Hormuz exemption, and the PM talked directly with Trump. The 'selective loosening' signal became a full diplomatic and energy realignment. The expectation was right in direction but wildly understated in magnitude. What came that was not expected: the Kurdish coalition splitting, the Khor Mor gas field being hit and a mass blackout following, the US formally requesting border closures, Iraq receiving a specific Hormuz pass, the PM's direct Trump talks, and the 'external parties' diplomatic framing. What this pattern says about our expectations being wrong for this country: we consistently underweight the structural fragility of the Kurdish north and overestimate the staying power of one-week diplomatic stories. The PUK-KDP tension was a known vulnerability that was always present, but we treated the disarmament announcement as the main Kurdish story and missed that the coalition itself could crack. We also underweight the speed at which a US-Iran escalation can pull Iraq into the centre of the action. A quiet banking note in the Wall Street Journal turned, in eight days, into a border-closure request and a Hormuz exemption. Our calibration for Iraq tends to be too slow: we expect gradualism, but the country's position between two great-power rivals means that shifts can come in a single week. Finally, we overestimate the half-life of symbolic events like the Pope's visit and the Tishreen anniversary. In Iraq, those stories burn bright for a few days and then fade, making room for the structural and external pressures that are always building underneath.
delta.driver: The single force pushing Iraq from the first photograph to the second is the intensifying US-Iran confrontation and Iraq's desperate attempt to stay in the middle of it. In the first photo, Baghdad was in a calm, outward-looking diplomatic mode: meeting the Syrian president, exploring a new oil route, managing high-profile court verdicts, and letting the Pope's Mosul visit generate soft power. By the second photo, the US and Iran had escalated to the point where Washington was asking Baghdad to close its borders with Tehran and negotiating a specific Hormuz exemption for Iraqi oil, while Iran was hitting Kurdish infrastructure and opposition groups that it blames for hosting its adversaries. This external squeeze is reshaping Iraq's internal politics from the top down. The PUK-KDP coalition in the north, which had been holding together through a fragile power-sharing arrangement, cracked under the combined stress of hosting Iranian opposition figures, absorbing the economic hit of the Khor Mor strike, and competing over who gets to negotiate with Baghdad and with the outside world. The PM's 'external parties using Iraqi soil' remark is the diplomatic expression of a country that is being used as a stage, a corridor, and a target simultaneously, and that does not want to be any of those things. The energy crisis in the north, the border-closure request, and the Hormuz exemption are all facets of the same underlying dynamic: two great powers are repositioning, and Iraq's geography, oil, and political fragmentation make it the ground on which they do it. The motion from photo one to photo two is not a series of unrelated events; it is one country being pulled into a confrontation it did not start and trying to keep its internal pieces from falling apart while it does so.

crystal.reasoning:
Starting from the present: Iraq enters this week with three interlocking crises. The Kurdish coalition has already cracked, with one major party formally quitting and the question of two separate administrations now openly on the table. The Khor Mor gas field is down, production halted, and a mass blackout is affecting hundreds of thousands in late autumn when heating demand is rising. And Baghdad is in the middle of a US-Iran standoff, having been asked to close most of its Iran border crossings while simultaneously receiving a rare Hormuz exemption and holding direct talks with the Trump administration. The PM's 'external parties using Iraqi soil' remark captures the diplomatic posture: Baghdad is being used as stage, corridor, and target, and it does not want any of those roles.

Extending each theme along its motion. The Kurdish political fracture is in an acceleration phase. The coalition did not just crack; a party formally quit, and Al Jazeera is asking whether we are back to two administrations. The natural next step in this motion is not a slow negotiation but a formal announcement or a visible split in governance: separate cabinet sessions, separate budget proposals, or one party declaring a 'shadow government.' The Yazidi/PKK disarmament that Baghdad was pushing becomes more complicated if there are now two Kurdish authorities to negotiate with. I expect the federal government in Baghdad to be pulled into mediating, which creates a new layer of tension: does Baghdad recognize one government or both, and what does that mean for the federal budget and the oil-revenue sharing formula? The motion is clearly from 'fragile unity held together by inertia' to 'open institutional split,' and the wind tells me I should not underestimate the speed of this.

The energy crisis in Kurdistan is moving from a single strike to a sustained supply problem. Khor Mor is one of the largest gas sources for the Kurdish grid. Losing it in November, with heating season starting, means the blackout is not a one-day event but a multi-day or multi-week crisis until production resumes or alternative supply is arranged. The motion from 'one drone hit a gas field' to 'hundreds of thousands lose power' suggests the next step is emergency logistics: importing electricity from Turkey or Iraq, deploying generators, and the political blame game. If the actor behind the strike (most likely Iran or a proxy) wants to escalate, a second strike on a different energy target is more likely than a random event, because the pattern is deliberate escalation. But the wind also warns me not to over-project a single dramatic event; the story may be more about the grinding management of the blackout than about a second explosion.

The US-Iran-Iraq diplomatic triangle is in an implementation phase. The US asked for border closures; that is now a logistical and political task for Baghdad. The Hormuz exemption is secured, which is a win, but it also makes Iraq more visible in the energy chokepoint story. The PM's talks with Trump are done for now, but the wind tells me I should not expect a multi-week diplomatic saga from a single phone call. The border-closure implementation, however, has a longer half-life because it involves merchants, border towns, Shia parties who benefit from Iran trade, and the daily logistics of which gates open and which close. I expect domestic pushback on the border issue to be more visible than further US-Iran headline drama.

Correcting for the wind. My past errors for Iraq are: being too slow (expecting gradualism when the country shifts in a week), underweighting Kurdish structural fragility (treating the PUK-KDP split as a background risk rather than an imminent event), overestimating the half-life of symbolic events, and underweighting the speed at which a US-Iran escalation pulls Iraq into the center. Applying those corrections: I should give the Kurdish split a higher probability of a visible, formal development this week than I would in a 'normal' forecast. I should not expect the Pope, the Tishreen anniversary, or the DNO Syria pipeline to resurface. I should expect the border-closure story to generate domestic political friction faster than I would normally predict. I should not bet on a full US-Iran war, but I should give a second drone strike a higher probability than a random event would suggest.

The single force pushing Iraq forward this week is the same driver that moved it last week: the US-Iran confrontation is the external pressure, and Iraq's internal fragmentation is the internal vulnerability, and the two are now interacting in real time. The Kurdish split is not just a domestic story; it is a story about who gets to negotiate with Baghdad, with Iran, with the US, and with the outside world, and that is exactly the question the US-Iran standoff is forcing. The blackout is not just an energy story; it is a political weapon that makes the Kurdish split more urgent because the public is cold and angry and wants someone to blame. The border closures are not just a diplomatic request; they are a domestic political cost that Baghdad has to pay in votes, in merchant protests, and in Shia party loyalty.

What I would not bet on: a full cabinet collapse in Baghdad, a major corruption verdict dominating the news, the DNO Syria pipeline making a headline, a major protest wave in Basra or Baghdad, a formal US-Iran war declaration, or the French ISIS trial story resurfacing in a big way. The week is too dominated by the Kurdish fracture, the blackout, and the border diplomacy for those to compete. What I would not bet on but should keep as a possibility: a second drone strike, a formal two-administration announcement from Kurdistan, and a visible Iraqi domestic pushback against the border closures.
crystal.forecast:
Theme 1: Kurdish political split becomes visible and formal. The PUK-KDP coalition collapse that began last week will likely produce a concrete institutional development this week: either a formal announcement of separate governing structures, a public budget dispute, or one party declaring a 'shadow cabinet.' Baghdad will be pulled into mediating, and the question of whether the federal government recognizes one or both Kurdish authorities will become a live political issue. The Yazidi/PKK disarmament process, which was progressing under a unified Kurdish command, will face complications if there are now two governments to coordinate with. Confidence: high that this dominates the Kurdish news cycle; medium that a formal split announcement lands within the seven days rather than being a slow bleed.

Theme 2: Kurdish energy crisis deepens and becomes a political story. The Khor Mor blackout will not be resolved in a single week. I expect emergency power arrangements to be announced (imports from Turkey or the Iraqi federal grid, generator deployments), public frustration to grow in Sulaymaniyah and Erbil, and the blackout to become a political weapon in the PUK-KDP split, with each side blaming the other for the energy vulnerability. A second drone strike on Kurdish infrastructure is more likely than a random event given the deliberate escalation pattern, but the week's energy story is more about the grinding management of the blackout than about a single dramatic explosion. Confidence: high that the blackout and its management remain a top-three story; medium for a second strike.

Theme 3: Border-closure implementation generates domestic friction. The US request to close most Iraq-Iran border crossings will move from diplomatic language to logistical reality this week. I expect which specific crossings close, which stay open, and the practical chaos at the gates. Domestic pushback will come from Shia political parties (who benefit from Iran trade), border-town merchants, and the general public. Baghdad will try to frame the closures as temporary and security-driven, but the political cost will be visible. The Hormuz exemption will be referenced as a consolation, but it does not offset the border-town pain. Confidence: medium-high that the border story generates visible domestic political friction; medium that it produces a headline-level protest or parliamentary debate.

Theme 4: Baghdad's federal government shows strain but holds. The federal cabinet and parliament will be pulled into managing the Kurdish split, the border closures, and the energy crisis simultaneously. I expect a parliamentary session or a cabinet statement addressing at least one of these issues, and the PM's 'external parties' narrative will be refined or repeated in a new context. A full cabinet collapse is unlikely, but visible tension between the Shia bloc, the Sunni bloc, and the Kurdish representatives will be more audible. Confidence: medium that the federal government remains functional but visibly stretched; low for a cabinet reshuffle or no-confidence motion this week.

Theme 5: Security posture remains tense but contained. The drone threat in the north will continue to shape the security narrative. I expect at least one more reference to the Khor Mor strike or a related security incident, and the PMF or military will issue statements about air defense readiness. A major new attack on Baghdad's Green Zone is possible but not the most likely scenario; the pattern of strikes has moved north. The US-Iran standoff will keep the security story in the background, but I do not expect a full-scale military engagement this week. Confidence: medium for at least one security-related headline; low for a major new attack on central Baghdad.

Less-likely surprises the motion makes more probable: a formal two-administration declaration from one of the Kurdish parties (we would normally say 'unlikely this fast,' but the motion is clearly accelerating); a visible Iraqi Shia party public break with Baghdad over the border closures (the wind says we underestimate the speed of domestic political reactions); a second drone strike on a different Kurdish energy or political target (the escalation pattern makes this more likely than a random event); and a brief but audible US statement referencing Iraq's cooperation on the border closures (the wind says we underestimate how quickly Washington will make Iraq's role visible).

What I would not bet on: a full US-Iran war declaration or a major kinetic US strike on Iran this week; the DNO Syria oil pipeline story resurfacing as a headline; a major corruption verdict or court story dominating the news cycle; the Pope or Christian community story making a significant return; a full cabinet collapse in Baghdad; or a major protest wave in Basra or Baghdad triggered by the cost-of-living squeeze. The week is too dominated by the Kurdish fracture, the blackout, and the border diplomacy for those to compete for attention.
crystal.headline: Kurdish Split Deepens, Blackout Bites, Border Closures Sting
emoji_reasons: The Khor Mor gas field blackout is the most immediately felt, tangible crisis for hundreds of thousands of Iraqis in late autumn, and it will dominate daily life and headlines.
The PUK-KDP coalition collapse and the prospect of two separate Kurdish administrations is the week's biggest political drama and the clearest sign of structural fracture.
The US-Iran-Iraq diplomatic triangle, from border-closure requests to the Hormuz exemption to Trump-al-Zaidi talks, is the structural backdrop that shapes every other story.
crystal.tldr: Iraq's Kurdish north will face a visible political split and a sustained energy blackout this week, while Baghdad manages the domestic friction of closing its Iran border crossings under US pressure. The US-Iran standoff continues to squeeze Iraq from both sides, but a full war or a federal cabinet collapse is unlikely. The week's center of gravity is the Kurdish fracture and its energy consequences.
crystal.eli5:
Imagine a house where two brothers who used to share the kitchen are now arguing so loudly that one of them is packing his stuff into a separate room. That is what is happening in northern Iraq right now. The two biggest Kurdish political parties, who used to run the region together, are splitting apart. One of them has already walked out, and next week we will probably see them formally set up separate offices, separate budgets, and start blaming each other for the problems. It is like a family dinner where the two older siblings stop talking to each other and start setting up their own little tables.

At the same time, one of the main gas stations that powers the electricity for the whole Kurdish region got hit by a drone and stopped working. So now, in the middle of autumn when it is getting cold, hundreds of thousands of people are sitting in the dark, trying to find a way to heat their homes. Think of it like your house's main heater breaking down the first cold night of winter, and you have to figure out whether to buy a space heater, borrow one from a neighbor, or call the repair guy. Except the scale is a whole region, and the repair might take weeks.

In the middle of all this, the United States asked Iraq to close most of the roads and borders it shares with Iran, because the US and Iran are in a big argument right now and the US wants to make it harder for them to trade and move people. Iraq said okay, but now the shops and businesses along the border are getting angry because they used to sell and buy across that line every day. It is like if your school told you that the playground next door is closed, and now you have to share a smaller playground with everyone else. The Iraqi government is trying to keep everyone calm while also keeping a good relationship with both the US and Iran, which is like trying to be friends with two kids who are in a fight and both of them want you on their side. The most likely outcome for next week is that the Kurdish split gets more visible, the blackout keeps going, and the border towns get grumpy, but nothing as dramatic as a full war or a government falling apart.

judgment.reading_a: Forecast A structured the week around five to six threads and named the French ISIS sentences as 'the dominant story.' In reality, the French story was a small side-note (a TV5Monde piece on the convicts expressing regrets), not the center of gravity. A overestimated the Syria re-engagement: it expected a joint Baghdad-Damascus communique, a DNO-Syria technical update, and a Turkish reaction, none of which appeared in the week's headlines. The Tishreen anniversary gesture, the Yazidi disarmament logistics, and the Pope's lingering media presence all played out as background at best, which A roughly got right in scale. The graft conviction got the expected party-level murmuring but never surfaced as a headline. Where A went most wrong was in its security and US-Iraq read. It called security 'quiet by the standards of recent months' and limited the baseline to a single small incident, yet the week produced drone strikes on Iranian Kurdish opposition groups in Sulaymaniyah and east Erbil and a drone hit on the Khor Mor gas field that halted production and triggered a mass blackout across parts of Iraqi Kurdistan. A also said 'the US will remain a quiet presence' with only a possible Treasury follow-up on the bank wind-down, but in reality the US asked Iraq to shut most Iran border crossings, Iraq's foreign minister held talks with Trump, and Baghdad reached understandings with Washington to keep oil exports flowing through the Strait of Hormuz while Iran exempted Iraq from its own Hormuz restrictions. A's economy call of 'quiet except for the DNO-Syria thread' missed the Hormuz and border-crossing stories entirely. Finally, A declared the week 'a consolidation and reaction week, not a turning-point week,' yet the Kurdish power-sharing deal's collapse, with one of the two rival parties quitting the northern government and Al Jazeera openly asking whether Kurdistan could return to two separate administrations, was precisely the kind of turning-point event A said it would not bet on. The KDP friction A noted in the Yazidi-disarmament context is a faint echo of the broader KDP political rupture, but A never framed it as a standalone cabinet-level crisis.
judgment.reading_b: Forecast B organized the week into eight themed paragraphs and used a graduated probability language (almost certain, probable, possible, unlikely) that made its claims easier to hedge. The French diplomatic reaction, the Tishreen follow-through, the corruption-case fallout, the Pope and Christian community, and the DNO-Kurdistan oil thread all played out as minor or background stories, which B roughly calibrated correctly. B's security theme focused on the Green Zone and expected 'a second low-level drone or missile detected in the next few days.' The actual drone activity was real but shifted geographically: the strikes hit Kurdish opposition targets in Sulaymaniyah and east Erbil and then the Khor Mor gas field, not the Green Zone itself. B was in the right neighborhood (drones, low-level, nervousness in official statements) but pointed at the wrong province. B's banking-and-Iran theme expected a central-bank or finance-ministry follow-up on the WSJ wind-down story; the actual Iran-related news was far larger, involving Hormuz exemptions, border-crossing shutdowns, and direct Baghdad-Washington talks. B missed the Kurdish power-sharing collapse as a standalone theme entirely; none of its eight paragraphs addressed the PUK-KDP coalition breaking apart. B also did not anticipate the US-Iran-Iraq diplomatic triangle or the 'external parties using Iraqi soil' framing. However, B's hedging meant it never confidently predicted the week would be quiet or that the US would be a minor presence, so its reader was less blindsided than A's reader. B's 'less likely surprises' list included a minor Baghdad explosion and a surprise foreign-ministry statement, both of which were in the right spirit of the week's smaller items even if the big surprises were elsewhere. Overall B's picture was a follow-through week on existing threads, which was directionally plausible for the smaller stories but missed the three dominant events: the Kurdish political fracture, the drone escalation on infrastructure, and the US-Iran diplomatic squeeze on Baghdad.
judgment.comparison: Both forecasts were written as follow-up and consolidation pieces, and both missed the week's three actual dominant stories: the Kurdish power-sharing deal collapsing, the drone strikes on Kurdish opposition targets and the Khor Mor gas field (with the resulting mass blackout), and the US-Iran-Iraq diplomatic triangle involving Hormuz exemptions, border-crossing shutdowns, and Baghdad's high-level talks with Washington. Neither forecast had a dedicated theme for the KDP-PUK coalition breaking apart, which was the single biggest political event of the week. Neither anticipated the drone escalation hitting energy infrastructure rather than just a minor Baghdad incident. Neither saw the US going from 'quiet presence' to actively shaping Iraq's border and trade posture in the middle of a US-Iran standoff. On the smaller threads, both forecasts were roughly calibrated: the French ISIS sentences were a background story (A overestimated, B was closer), the Tishreen anniversary produced soft follow-through, the corruption verdicts generated party murmuring, the Pope's visit lingered in soft media coverage, and the DNO-Syria oil story did not produce the headline-level communique A expected. A's specific confident claims made it more visibly wrong: 'Security will be quiet,' 'The US will remain a quiet presence,' 'the dominant story will be the French ISIS sentences,' and 'a consolidation and reaction week, not a turning-point week' were all directly contradicted.
